flags.why: "both Grey and Green Linnets": the name is shared, so "Grey Linnets" can't be copied from this phrase. "Grey" is a fragment; the chunk also prints "Grey\nLinnets" (Skerryvore), which the rules allow. The text isn't misprinted, so not gutenberg.

"enormous numbers crossed in the autumn, commencing Aug. 7th ...; from thence to Sept. 18th, almost daily": the clause continues "crossed", so these birds are passing. Quote should start at "enormous numbers crossed".

"late in afternoon. Meadow Pipits, great flights. Tree Pipits less": whether the time reaches past a full stop to the Tree Pipits is unclear, so null is defensible. (The stop after "afternoon" may be a transcription slip.)
"scattered flocks of Wild Ducks, about seven in number": a vague count. Either "scattered flocks" or "about seven" will do; the checker's string also takes in the bird name.
"At Whitby L.H., Sept. 27th, 10\na.m., a large flock of small birds containing many Robins": the time is stated for these birds and was left out.
"one passing\nS.E.": the rules give the example "passing S." as a direction, so the verb is kept. The checker's "S.E." tidies it.
"one struck and caught": one observation per behaviour, so "struck" is right for this one. "caught" should be a second observation (check that it exists), not a replacement.
The text reads "7.80 p.m." and the print reads 7.30. The record copies the text exactly; the slip is in the transcription.
"Both were captured": "Both" is the quantity word printed for the caught birds, like "eight killed". "two" belongs to "flew on board".
The text reads "_Tardus Naumanii_" and the checker reads Turdus in the print. The record copies the text; the slip is in the transcription (italics are ignored).
"At Godrevy, Oct. 4th, 1 to 2 a.m., mod. E.N.E. breeze, ... were seen, and three birds killed": one entry, and the time covers the killed birds. The wind was taken from it but the time was left out.
"a great number of Larks, 8 p.m., light E.S.E., haze. Great numbers struck": the struck clause continues this one; it already took "Larks" and the weather from it, so the time goes with them.
"three and a Starling caught": this observation is the Starling, with count "a", which is right. The Chaffinch "three" should be its own observation, not this one.
For the Starling observation the count is "a Starling", so "a" is right. "three" is the Chaffinches' count, in a separate observation.
"Oct. 25th, mod. W. breeze, till midnight, some struck and fell overboard; three and a Starling caught": the caught clause continues the entry and shares its time.
